Behavioral safety benchmarks are validated by predictive accuracy, not by construct identification. We introduce an identification audit for such benchmarks, and show that the common instructed-lie paradigm fails it. \textbf{We do not ask whether LLMs can detect deception; we ask whether current benchmarks provide evidence that they do.} The standard paradigm scores behavioral LLM deception detectors in one setting, \emph{instructed roleplay}: the model is told to lie, and the instruction that produces the deception also produces the compliance, so a detector can score high while measuring whether the model was \emph{instructed} to lie. The reason is structural: \textbf{no experiment that intervenes only on the instruction can separate a detector response mediated by deception from one mediated by instruction-following}, both being descendants of that instruction. A deception-attribution reading therefore needs $\tau_D$, the effect of \emph{deception}, which the identified $\tau_E$---the \emph{instruction}'s effect---neither bounds nor signs, so no gain in accuracy, scale, or detector sophistication resolves it. \textbf{This is an identification problem, not a generalization problem: generalization can be perfect while identification still fails.} We turn it into a falsifiable audit protocol: five criteria we propose as necessary before accuracy licenses a deception claim---three alternative-explanation diagnostics, one construct-validity test no instructed design can supply, and one robustness test.

Fixed elicitation itself is not new---trained belief-verified organisms have it---but it has not been used as the \emph{construct-validity criterion} for reading instructed-benchmark accuracy.

Reimplemented from scratch, the standard black-box behavioral detector reaches 81.7\% on instructed-lie trials and 53.7\% once both conditions receive identical prompts. A pre-registered replication on a disjoint claim set and probe bank then \textbf{leaves no detectable above-chance discrimination on any of the six targets} (97.0\%$\to$\textbf{43.3\%}), as does a white-box linear probe on residual activations in two model families, at 100.0\% instructed, at chance equalized, and matched by surface features (92.5--99.0\%). \textbf{The accuracy the benchmark is scored on is reachable with no learned features at all}: a parameter-free lexical rule reaches 69--80\%---\emph{surface-accessible accuracy}, not a decomposition of the detector's signal. We then audit both public rollout releases for the one criterion that removes the elicitation confound: \textbf{nine of ten rollout sets cannot supply it} for a deployed-observable rule; on the tenth our rule is \textbf{null} while \textbf{the corpus authors' own judge, run verbatim on the same visible text, does separate deception there} (AUROC 0.71/0.94), so the null is the instrument's, not the criterion's; scoring the \emph{hidden} scaffold instead reports $+84.3$\,pp---\textbf{annotation-channel leakage}, the model echoing ``incorrect'' from its own instruction. A second release---35 cells, five generator families, fully pre-registered---fails differently: its label grades the very text both instruments read, so passing is \textbf{construct recovery}. We claim identification, not attribution, and \textbf{equalization may remove the deception with the confound}. Because \textbf{no public release we audited supplies all five}, we built materials that do: with deception operationalized independently of the detector's input, prior work's battery separates operationally verified deception on three of five targets---all three with power ($p\!\leq\!0.006$; two nulls underpowered)---of which \textbf{a blinded re-run replicates two, so the standing count is two of five}, with \textbf{one of five \emph{new} targets positive}. \textbf{The canonical benchmark is non-identifying, and a deception-\emph{associated} signal is nevertheless detectable under a valid fixed-elicitation design}---on \emph{some} targets, still not $\tau_D$---\textbf{rung~4 of five}, on the ladder the protocol defines. \textbf{Scope: English, instructed-roleplay evaluations, open-weight models 3B--70B.}

\paragraph{Relation to prior work.} White-box probes read deception from activations~\citep{zou2023representation, burns2022discovering, azaria2023internal}; the black-box line's closest instance---our primary audit target---is \citet{pacchiardi2023catch}, and we audit both paradigms (§\ref{sec:td_vs_fd}). Three concurrent evaluations~\citep{kretschmar2025liarsbench, cooney2026didyoulie, hopkins2026liedetectors} find lie detectors fail to \textbf{generalize} beyond the regime they were fit in. That is a generalization question; ours is the prior one: instructed-lie accuracy is \textbf{not merely poorly generalizing but uninterpretable as evidence about deception}, because the intervention moves deception and compliance together---so generalization can be perfect while identification still fails. \textbf{Fixed elicitation is also not what we claim to introduce}---\citet{cooney2026didyoulie}'s trained organisms have it and go \emph{beyond} it, with $D$ \emph{set} rather than observed. \textbf{Our novelty is using it as the missing construct-validity criterion for reading instructed-benchmark accuracy}, and auditing whether public artifacts supply it---a gap \textbf{invisible in a benchmark's own output}, the reported accuracy being the same number whether or not the criterion holds. Appendix~\ref{app:related_work} places all five kinds---instructed-lie benchmarks, generalization studies, belief-verified model organisms, the public rollout corpora, and four adjacent constructs---against requirements~(i)--(v) (Appendix Table~\ref{tab:prior_work_criteria}).

\paragraph{How the criteria divide: 3 + 1 + 1.} Two axes: 3+1+1 is \emph{who can apply} a criterion; by \emph{what it identifies}, \textbf{1 and 4 are fundamental and 2, 3, 5 supporting}. \textbf{The five are not claimed to characterize every valid deception benchmark}---they rule out specific alternative explanations. \textbf{Passing criterion~4 is necessary, not sufficient}: at fixed $E$ deception varies \emph{naturally}, so any latent $U$ with $U\!\to\!D$ and $U\!\to\!S$ survives it---criterion~4 removes the \emph{elicitation} confound and no other, and what it establishes is deception-associated behavior \emph{conditional on the operational belief criterion}. The output is a verdict on a benchmark, not a detector: \textbf{the protocol falsifies validity claims rather than certifying them}. Our own instructed materials fail 1, 3 and 5; EXP-C4 (§\ref{sec:external_audit}) supplies criterion~4 at a prompt fixed by construction.

\paragraph{So we built one, and prior work's own battery separates deception in it (EXP-C4, \emph{pre-registered}).} One system prompt per claim presents a knowledge-screened false fact as an authoritative internal reference and \textbf{never instructs deception}; the target asserts it---deception, the belief screen showing it holds the negation---or corrects it, with $D$ graded by a cross-family judge from the \textbf{on-claim answer alone} ($\alpha\!=\!0.728$ vs.\ hand coding) while the detector reads only the 16-probe vector, so all of~(i)--(v) hold; 125--160 graded trials per target. \textbf{On three of five targets---all three in which the design had power---the battery separates operationally verified deception at byte-identical elicitation}: 0.650/0.807/0.903 against majority 0.575/0.594/0.682, $p\!\leq\!0.006$ under claim-grouped folds and within-claim permutation; the other two are \textbf{null and uninformative} (MDE $\ge\!0.80$). All deceptive trials still hold the true fact re-queried outside the reference---not belief revision (H3, pre-registered). \emph{Stratified observational} at fixed $E$: deception-\emph{associated}, not $\tau_D$ (Appendix~\ref{app:crit4_ours}). A blinded, Holm-corrected re-run (EXP-C4B) replicates two of the three positives---not the weakest, which falls below its own baseline---\textbf{so the standing count is two of five}---and only one of five \emph{new} targets, so this is not a design property that reappears on arbitrary targets (Appendix~\ref{app:crit4b}). \textbf{Criterion~5 (transfer) is exploratory}: 2 of 5, cross-model only, not part of the argument (Appendix~\ref{app:crit4_transfer}). \textbf{Three stages, and the trend is the result.} Instructed elicitation is high and stable (81.7\%, 97.0\% pooled), equalizing it collapses accuracy to chance (53.7\%, 43.3\%), and at fixed $E$ the signal returns on \emph{a subset} of targets---\textbf{removing the confound makes detection markedly less stable across targets}, so instructed headline accuracy overstates how much of detection is invariant. \textbf{The purpose of criterion~4 is not to establish that deception is generally detectable; it is to establish that the canonical benchmark's failure is not an impossibility result.}

\textbf{We establish:} \textbf{(1)}~instructed-roleplay designs identify the effect of the \emph{instruction} and cannot bound that of \emph{deception}---an \emph{identification} failure, not a detector failure; \textbf{(2)}~the confound is \emph{active}, not hypothetical, across \emph{three} detector paradigms, while the score moves inside a single deception label; \textbf{(3)}~across \emph{both} public rollout releases---ten rollout sets and 35 further cells---nine of the ten cannot express the one criterion that removes the elicitation confound on a deployed-observable channel, and the closest cells fail in three distinct ways: an instrument-specific null, \textbf{annotation-channel leakage}, and \textbf{construct recovery}; and \textbf{(4)}~on materials we built to satisfy all of §1's (i)--(v), prior work's own battery \emph{does} separate operationally verified deception on three of five targets---all three in which the design had power ($p\!\leq\!0.006$; two underpowered nulls, MDE $\ge\!0.80$); a blinded re-run replicates two of those three, and not the weakest---\textbf{so the standing count is two of five}---while on five \emph{new} targets it is positive on one (EXP-C4B, Appendix~\ref{app:crit4b}). \textbf{The canonical instructed benchmark is therefore non-identifying, and a deception-\emph{associated} signal is nevertheless detectable under a valid fixed-elicitation design}---on \emph{some} targets, not $\tau_D$.

\textbf{We establish:} \textbf{(1)}~instructed-roleplay designs identify the effect of the \emph{instruction} and cannot bound that of \emph{deception}---an \emph{identification} failure, not a detector failure; \textbf{(2)}~the confound is \emph{active}, not hypothetical, across \emph{three} detector paradigms, while the score moves inside a single deception label; \textbf{(3)}~across \emph{both} public rollout releases---ten rollout sets and 35 further cells---nine of the ten cannot express the one criterion that removes the elicitation confound on a deployed-observable channel, and the closest cells fail in three distinct ways: an instrument-specific null, \textbf{annotation-channel leakage}, and \textbf{construct recovery}; and \textbf{(4)}~on materials we built to satisfy all of §1's (i)--(v), prior work's own battery \emph{does} separate operationally verified deception on three of five targets---all three in which the design had power; a blinded re-run replicates two, plus one of five \emph{new} targets, and \textbf{a pre-registered covariate audit withdraws one of the two, leaving one of five standing} (EXP-C4B/AE, Appendices~\ref{app:crit4b},~\ref{app:covariate_audit}); and \textbf{(5)}~\textbf{the audit changes \emph{which} behavior indicates deception}---the instructed benchmark's best probe is inert at fixed $E$, and another replaces it (EXP-AD). \textbf{The canonical instructed benchmark therefore fails to identify deception, while a fixed-elicitation design reveals \emph{target-dependent} deception-associated signals}---not $\tau_D$.
